items.note: Abstract: combined climate and land-use change reduced mean monsoon streamflow of the Betwa (semi-arid catchment in Central India) by 16% in 2001-2020 versus 1982-2000; further decreases of 39-47% and 31-47% projected, with monsoon rainfall down 30-35% and 23-30%.

Regional context for Central India: open forest and vegetation cover diminished while agricultural land increased (1981-2006), and mean Indian Summer Monsoon Rainfall over Central India declined by 10-20% from 1950-2015.

The Upper Betwa catchment has experienced decreased mean monsoon rainfall, more extreme rainfall events, rising mean temperature and LU-LC change; meteorological dry events increased after 2000 and are projected to intensify.

Betwa River rises in Raisen district and joins the Yamuna in Hamirpur district; upstream largely intermittent, perennial in the last 85 km; Upper Betwa single-thread channel 127 km long, catchment 9322 km2, semi-arid to dry sub-humid.
Upper Betwa catchment: summer maximum temperature 40-45 °C (March-May), winter minimum down to 2 °C (November-February); about 92% of rainfall falls in the monsoon (June-September).
Topography of the Upper Betwa catchment ranges from 376 to 669 m above mean sea level; higher in the west (451-669 m) than the east (376-550 m).

items.note: Land use of the Upper Betwa catchment: agricultural land 76%, forest 14%, urban 3%, open land 4%, water 2%; from 1990-2020 agriculture, built-up and water increased by 3%, 2% and 1% while forest and open land fell by 4% and 2%.
Increase in agricultural and urban land linked to population growth (catchment population up 60% from 1991 to 2011); more water bodies attributed to dam construction in 2011-2013.
Cumulative Indian summer monsoon rainfall in the catchment shows a declining trend of 2 mm from 1980-2020.
Between 2001-2020 and 1980-2000, meteorological dry events (SPI) increased by 15% while wet and normal events decreased by 4% and 11%; per SDI dry and wet events up 4%, normal down 9%.

Streamflow hydrograph of the Upper Betwa catchment: rising limb begins in June and falls after September; the catchment receives more than 90% of rainfall in the monsoon; flow is low pre- and post-monsoon.
Mean streamflow decreased by 16% in 2001-2020 against 1982-2000; maximum and minimum streamflow fell from 1079 and 139 m3/s to 673 and 127 m3/s.
Projected mean monsoon streamflow decrease of about 39-47% (2023-2060) and 31-41% (2061-2100), with monsoon rainfall decrease of 30-35% and 23-30%, relative to 1982-2020.
Annual average flow fell from 312 m3/s (1982-2000) to 281 m3/s (2001-2020); mean monsoon streamflow 371 m3/s in dry years and 688 m3/s in wet years.
Agriculture in the catchment is primarily rain-fed, so rainfall deviations affect crop yield; monsoon rainfall has a high correlation (0.8) with Kharif crop production anomalies.

Conclusions: a transition from wetter to drier hydro-climatic conditions is evident in the upper Betwa catchment; mean monsoon streamflow fell 16% in 2001-2020, is projected to fall by 39-47% and 31-41%, and water scarcity is likely to aggravate.
